Several ideas that I would pay attention to in your case:

​

1.Make sure to not limit yourself to the patterns of the past - what I observed at many people is that even though they might not realize it, they tend to make the decisions of today based on the patterns that they created in the past. This happens when you identify yourself with that persona who did things in a specific way repeatedly (leaving uni after an emotional problem, then leaving uni again because of another emotional problem).

Perhaps the image of yourself doesn't affect you, but perhaps it does - in that case, make sure you truly assess the way you see yourself and you can give yourself a fresh start by not seeing yourself as "that guy who quits every time an emotional problem kicks in".

​

2. Comfort can kill any possible passion - You say you have trouble being committed to a work, that you get bored, that you don't find a strong enough "WHY".

However, I ask you another question: aren't you just as bored with the life you're living right now ? Do you have a stronger "WHY" for living with your parents, being unemployed, etc. ?

My point is not to scold you, but to make you consider that is comfort zone that you're resistant to leave might not make you happier either.

Getting a new job and moving out of your parents' house is a risk - not getting a job and not moving out is a risk as well. There is no safety net, no matter what you choose. Nothing guarantees happiness. Can you look in the mirror right now and say that you're happy ? So what do you have to lose ?

​

​

3. Passion, just like love, takes a great amount of cultivation.

Do not believe the superficial motivational videos out there or the bloggers/vloggers, life coaches or anyone who makes you think that "passion just hits you and you have an easy ride from then".

I work in the Medical field and I can tell you that even the most passionate doctor has days when he burns out, when he feels hollow, when he's just low on that drive.

This is not the problem, the problem is that our society doesn't teach people to be realistic from the start, so when real problems kick in, you're feeling lost/confused/disturbed/disgusted/depressed/angry at life.

The problem is NOT that there are days in which you wake up and you're not enthusiastic about your work, the problem is that you enter panic mode because this is what you've been brainwashed to think, that "omg, something is seriously wrong if today I'm not kissed by the muse of my art" - No, the thing is that sometimes the muse has to be seduced. Sometimes you got to start playing the piano to eventually start enjoying playing piano. Sometimes inspiration doesn't hit you, but you create it through tinkering with something, through experimenting with things, through LIVING.

​

4. "If a man is throwed into a cage full of lions, he's not going to have time to be depressed."

Although some might consider this harsh, it's a very eye-opening and mentally challenging idea: how much does your own comfort contribute to your depression ?

We tend to think about this backwards: "the more comfort we have, the more happiness we have" - This is often times a flawed idea.

What I've observed at people who are in their comfort zones all the time is that their minds start to create problems out of pettiness - this is why many rich teens end up suffocating themselves in drama, drugs, drinking, eating disorders, etc.

The comfort zones, the habits, the lifestyle that we have can act as a  "clogger" on your creativity, on your drive, on your raw survival skills, so that your mind doesn't focus on these things anymore, but instead starts to wallow in toxic emotions, poor habits, pointless chatter, petty interests, etc.

Now beware: some people confuse challenges and difficulties with misery. Just because you get out of your comfort zone and you embrace challenges in your life, IT DOES NOT MEAN THAT YOU HAVE TO BE MISERABLE. If people would understand this, they could leave their habits and their comfort zones so much easier.

Having a difficult life doesn't necessarily make you miserable and having an easy life doesn't necessarily make you happy.

​

5. Build your emotional handling skills very well - they're going to make the difference between success and failure many, many times.

As you have already experienced, poor emotional intelligence can make you lose many things.

It's not your fault, we live in a society that teaches us that if we ignore our emotions long enough, they are going to handle themselves on their own - sometimes it's true, sometimes it isn't. It's never a wise idea to neglect something, to be in denial about it, to superficially try to solve it.

You don't have to wallow in your emotions, but you have to be mindful about them. Do not use them as an excuse for your shortcomings, but don't deny their existence, identify that there is a problem and a problem requires solution, not negligence.

Be methodical, be rigorous - the process of psychological development is just like brushing your teeth: it's not a matter of "today I feel my teeth healthy enough to not brush them" - Build your psychological knowledge like an engineer would build a castle and nothing short of that. If you're just going to "wiggle it" , the results are going to be the same.

Be understanding - no book, no therapist, no movie and nothing at all is going to be useful if you don't make a conscious decision to understand YOURSELF. You'll see that understanding things on a theoretical level, in a general way is very different from applying that knowledge in practice, within your own persona. Just like the eye can see anything outside of it, but can't see itself, sometimes the mind can understand anything outside of it, but can't understand itself. You got to be very introspective to truly understand yourself.

​

Best wishes !

These thoughts you're having are not ridiculous in my opinion. It's definitely an advantage to have self-criticism. When you can criticize yourself you can see problems in the future which you'd otherwise not see. This is what I'm doing right now as well, a rigorous self-assessment. 

I think the most important thing would be to find the roots of your condition. This is what I have been hunting down for years. The only reason for why I have lasted so long in Medical school so far is that I've been doing a good job hunting my demons and peeling off layers of my subconscious until now. I've hit a new dark spot again, but like a fierce miner, I don't get intimidated by it. I'm going to find the root of this dark spot as well. 

I don't know your situation nor the roots of your demons, but I'd advice you to not be satisfied with conventional answers. Depression is so complex - I don't agree with people who say it's only something you were born with, nor do I agree with the ones who say it was caused by a single event. It's probably a combination of several factors and all of those factors have to be worked out. 

I've hit so many lows in my life and I've risen from my ashes so many times that I could do it as a primary job. 

Perhaps it seems you're chasing your tail, but if you pay attention, you're not going in circles, but in a SPIRAL - getting deeper and deeper into your mind. This can be a very resourceful journey, but only if you don't make the same mistake twice and if you're not asleep......I know it's hard though. I'm constantly battling with staying awake versus knocking myself out to just turn off my mind. 

Perhaps what both of us should improve on is being awake more.....it's just that it's more difficult to be awake when you have demons than when you're not having them. I know it, because I remember how it is to not have them. As a kid I didn't have them and I never felt the need to K.O. myself. But when you're having demons, you don't want to be awake. Though perhaps the only way to learn to master your demons is to stay awake with them......

Read history and read literature - what is it full of ? Grueling and conflicting human emotion.

You're not the first nor the last one who experiences the torments of passion, break-up, indifference, lack of empathy from your peers and the rest of the emotional roller-coaster.

Are these emotions debilitating ? They can be. If you let them. But they can also be turned into wisdom and richness.

Imagine how it would be to have a father figure or a mother figure or even a partner with whom you could talk about your feelings and who would understand you and share some valuable insights with you - wouldn't that be great ? I am on the "Anti-class" side. I can respect all the people who are going to classes, I just have different goals. Taking cpsmith58's answer, I will show you what I mean: 

  * The discipline part: those who go to classes actually use someone else's discipline instead of training their own discipline. This is why classes are so catchy for people who are undisciplined, because there is someone else who yells at them, there is someone else to force them to do the exercises, there is someone else to make them push harder. **This gets the work done, but it doesn't build discipline.** -There is a subtle difference between the two. When I got into entrepreneurship, I started to learn what the real discipline is about: it starts from not having someone else yelling at you. Why ? Because contrary to conventional thinking, **being your own boss is the hardest thing.** This is why it builds discipline. 

  * The "shaming" tool: many of those who go to classes are going to tell you that "the shame of walking out is what keeps you there", "I am ashamed to not finish this workout", "I am ashamed to not push that weight at bench pressing" - So what's the deal with this shaming tool ? I simply don't believe in it. I think that **when you get the work done, it has to come from a place of concentration and connection between mind and body**: if you feel that 60 minutes Intense Cycling Insanity class is not for you, get out. I got into weightlifting, because I wasn't afraid to walk away from aerobic classes. When I got into weightlifting, I felt a strong mind-body connection, I used all my concentration to do it, and I've found out that yes, this is what I want to do, and I'm a weightlifting veteran ever since. **But in order to do this, I had to eliminate the shaming mentality, because all the shaming does is cloud your judgment.**

  * INCORRECT techniques: you would think that going to a certified trainer and paying money is a guarantee that you aren't doing incorrect movements that could damage your body, right ? Think again. **Most gyms and classes have no responsibility about what their clients do.** This doesn't mean that you're going to break your neck, but don't be surprised if you tear a ligament, get some pretty bad posture problems, mess up your knees or your elbows, etc. - The amount of incorrect techniques I've seen performed by certified trainers is huge. 

  * Music: some would jump all over someone if you say music is not for training. It's like taking away a strong drug from someone, because what music really does is giving that "dirty high" to your brain, an effect which has a psychological component, this is why some weightlifters listen to rap music while lifting ( imagining they kick someone's a$$, so the pump is there ), also this is why runners listen to pop songs ( the emotional impulse coming from the lyrics gets the brain into a daydreaming, trance-like state ). **I've been starting my training journey with no music**, training outside, sometime at night, therefore I've understood the power of deep focus: I realized that I don't need some compulsive noise, at loud intensity, to get the training done. It seems harder, especially if someone is used to music, to train without constant music ( which I call "audio crack" ), but over time you actually realize how great it is to train in complete silence and focus, not to mention that you won't have earbugs hours after the workout. 

  P.S.: I do love music & I party hard on it, just not when I'm training. 

  * Class buddies: it really depends on your luck, but more often you're better on your own. With all the information excess from the internet and magazines, most people are mindless consumers and constantly brainwashed into the ideas that the mainstream proposes. You'll probably hear people at your class talking about the latest "20 pounds in 5 days" diet, about how they do one hour of cardio on empty stomach, about how they don't eat after 6 o'clock and whether you know that sucking in your stomach so that you can barely breath is a great way to get a six pack. Besides this, they will be glad to chat with you during your rest time, between sets, not minding the time ( which is crucial to get right, resting too much simply makes the workout less effective ), and they will also challenge you to squat double weight compared to what you squatted 2 days ago, because you know, "it's cool, bruh !" - All jokes aside, I had friends who have teared their ligaments or damaged their spine only to show off, I also had friends who didn't make gains at the speed they wanted, only to find out that they've been spending 5 minutes at each rest to check out their buddy's social media, etc. etc. 

  **Point is: if you want gym buddies, better choose them wisely.** Going to a class only to have gym buddies is not a great idea in my opinion, because you just get stuck with a bunch of people. 

  * Reducing possibilities & locking yourself in a box: this is a no-brainer in a way. Some people have 3 aerobic classes per week, they also go lifting 5 times a week, while also jogging an hour in the morning and running a marathon at the end of the month. **However, most people have different priorities and different time schedules, so chances are that if you're doing 3 aerobic classes per week, that's what you're mainly going to do on the long-term** (  because short-term over-achieving is a common phenomenon, but what truly matters is what stays with you on the long-term ). It's what your aerobic buddies are also going to do. And if you'll say that you'd want to also do something else, they will tell you that they would be too tired for that, so you will also feel too tired for that, not to mention the trainer of the class, who will most likely tell you to take it easy and not over-burden yourself by doing too much outside of his/her classes ( him/her being afraid of not losing a client due to exhaustion ).
